sentences.text: Ichthyornis is an extinct genus of toothed, seabird-like ornithuran named for its fish-like vertebrae. Its name means "fish-bird" because the bones in its spine resemble those found in fish. This bird is notable for having concave vertebrae in both the front and rear sections, a feature similar to that of some fish.
The animal had teeth only in the middle of its jaws, while the tips were toothless and covered by a beak. It was an extinct genus of toothed birds from the Late Cretaceous.

An average Ichthyornis specimen was about 24 cm long with a skeletal wingspan of approximately 43 cm. Its average size was similar to a pigeon, measuring 24 centimeters in length with a wingspan of about 43 centimeters excluding feather length.

The genus Ichthyornis was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1872. Ichthyornis was discovered in 1870 by Benjamin Franklin Mudge in the North Fork of the Solomon River in Kansas. The genus Ichthyornis was named by Marsh in 1872. Ichthyornis was originally discovered in 1870 by Benjamin Franklin Mudge, who recovered fossils from the Solomon River in Kansas, USA.

Studies of Ichthyornis brain casts show it had a relatively basal brain similar to Archaeopteryx and non-avian theropods. Ichthyornis had a palate that was remarkably similar to that of modern neognath birds.

Ichthyornis specimens from earlier eras were generally smaller than those from later periods, with fossils found in the Greenhorn Formation of Kansas dating to the early Turonian (about 93 million years ago) and in Saskatchewan dating to the Cenomanian (about 95 million years ago), though the species lived from the Cenomanian to the Campanian stages, between 100.5 and 72.2 million years ago.

Ichthyornis is thought to have been the Cretaceous equivalent of modern seabirds like gulls, petrels, and skimmers. Ichthyornis is thought to have been the ecological equivalent of modern seabirds like gulls, petrels, and shearwaters during the Cretaceous.

Marsh classified Ichthyornis in the new subclass Odontornithes and order Ichthyornithes due to its unique concave vertebrae and teeth. Due to its unique features like concave vertebrae on both sides and teeth, Marsh classified the bird into its own subclass called Odontornithes, meaning "toothed birds," and the new order Ichthyornithes (later Ichthyornithiformes). The genus Ichthyornis was originally placed in the subclass Odontotormae by Marsh in 1875.

In Julia Clarke's 2004 review, the former order Ichthyornithiformes and family Ichthyornithidae were superseded by the clade Ichthyornithes. Ichthyornis is close to the ancestors of modern birds, the Neornithes, but represents an independent lineage. The genus Ichthyornis belongs to the parent group Ichthyornithes.

Fossils of Ichthyornis are found in the Western Interior Seaway deposits across Alberta, Alabama, Kansas, New Mexico, Saskatchewan, and Texas. Earlier Ichthyornis remains date to the early Turonian (about 93 million years ago) in Kansas and the late Cenomanian in Saskatchewan. Ichthyornis lived in North America between 93 and 75 million years ago, while other sources indicate it lived from the Cenomanian to the Campanian stages, between 100.5 and 72.2 million years ago.
